paragraphs: This paper studies how an agent can learn a control policy by asking an expert to compare short examples of behavior. Each query shows runs from two policies starting at the same state, and the expert chooses the preferred trajectory. The objective is to recover the expert’s latent target policy while asking as few questions as possible.

The authors introduce a Bayesian model of this querying process. They then develop two methods that use the model to actively select comparisons. Query selection becomes part of learning: the agent chooses which pair of behaviors to present, rather than treating all possible comparisons as equally useful.

Experiments on four benchmark problems indicate that this approach can learn policies effectively from trajectory preferences. They also indicate that actively chosen queries can be substantially more efficient than randomly selected ones. The practical significance is that learning useful behavior need not depend on the expert specifying a policy directly; carefully selected judgments between short runs can provide an effective teaching signal.
neurips-2012-a-bayesian-approach-for-pol.tldr: A Bayesian model helps an agent learn control policies efficiently by actively choosing which pairs of trajectories an expert should compare.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of estimating a sparse inverse covariance matrix when there are very many variables. This estimation problem can recover the graph structure of a Gaussian Markov random field. Existing statistical guarantees motivate the estimator even with limited samples, but solving the large optimization problem remains a separate challenge.

The proposed method partitions the variables into smaller problems, solves those problems, and combines their solutions into an approximation of the original solution. The authors derive a bound on the distance between the approximate and original solutions. They then use that bound to guide a clustering algorithm that seeks effective partitions.

The approximation also provides a starting point for solving the full problem, making the decomposition useful beyond producing a rough answer. In a climate application with 10,000 nodes, the reported runtime falls from ten hours with QUIC to one hour with Divide and Conquer QUIC. This example demonstrates how a theoretically guided initialization can substantially accelerate the original estimation task.
neurips-2012-a-divide-and-conquer-method.tldr: Partitioning a large sparse inverse covariance problem produces a bounded approximation that can also accelerate solving the full problem.

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents using multiple hidden topics, with each topic associated with a distribution over words. This is more expressive than assigning each document to a single cluster, but it makes learning harder: the words are visible while the topics and their contributions remain hidden. The paper develops a simple, efficient procedure for recovering these hidden model parameters.

The method, Excess Correlation Analysis, uses low-order statistical moments and two singular value decompositions. For Latent Dirichlet Allocation, third-order word statistics suffice to recover both the topic-word distributions and the parameters governing topic mixtures. Such statistics can be estimated from documents containing only three words, so the method does not inherently require long documents.

The recovery guarantee applies to a wide class of topic models that includes LDA. A key computational feature is that the decompositions operate on matrices sized by the number of topics, rather than the vocabulary size. Since the number of topics is typically much smaller, this makes the central spectral operations comparatively compact and supports scalability.
neurips-2012-a-spectral-algorithm-for-la.tldr: Excess Correlation Analysis recovers parameters of a broad class of topic models using third-order statistics and two small spectral decompositions.

paragraphs: Parametric policy search improves a decision-making policy by adjusting its parameters in a Markov decision process. This paper examines two prominent approaches, Expectation Maximisation and natural gradient ascent. Its central question concerns how these methods choose a direction in parameter space, and whether their choices reveal a useful shared structure.

The authors show that the step directions of both methods are closely related to the direction produced by an approximate Newton method. This connection gives a common perspective on algorithms that otherwise appear distinct. It also motivates using the approximate Newton method itself as an alternative policy-search algorithm.

The analysis establishes desirable properties of the proposed algorithm that a naive application of Newton’s method lacks. Empirical results suggest strong convergence and robustness, with competitive performance against both Expectation Maximisation and natural gradient ascent. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of existing methods with a new optimization option. The reported experiments support that option’s promise, while the theoretical relationship explains why it belongs alongside the established approaches.
neurips-2012-a-unifying-perspective-of-p.tldr: A shared connection to approximate Newton steps unifies two policy-search methods and motivates a promising alternative optimization algorithm.

paragraphs: A dynamical system with a single attractor can generate robot motion toward a target and respond to disturbances without replanning. Its destination remains fixed, however. This paper combines several systems with different attractors, allowing a reach-to-grasp controller to have several possible grasping points on an object. Multiple destinations offer greater flexibility when unexpected perturbations occur.

The proposed Augmented-SVM partitions the state space using the region-separating ability of a support vector machine. It adds constraints derived from the individual dynamical systems. These constraints change the optimization problem and introduce a new class of support vectors that governs how the component dynamics are combined.

The resulting system minimizes deviation from the original dynamics and is stable at each attractor within a finite region of attraction. That regional qualification matters: the stated stability does not cover every possible state. Implementations on a simulated mobile robot with ten degrees of freedom demonstrate real-time motion generation and adaptation to perturbations as they happen.
neurips-2012-augmented-svm-automatic-spa.tldr: Augmented-SVM combines robot motion systems with multiple targets while preserving local attractor stability and supporting real-time adaptation in simulation.

paragraphs: Clustering noisy, scattered, high-dimensional data can be formulated through balanced cut problems. Continuous relaxations make these problems accessible to numerical optimization and can produce strong clustering results. This paper examines the relaxed Cheeger Cut objective, focusing on whether algorithms converge and what the local minima of that objective represent.

The authors provide rigorous convergence results for two algorithms: a new steepest descent method and a slightly modified Inverse Power Method. The steepest descent method has stronger theoretical convergence properties. In practice, however, the two methods perform equally, separating the strength of a mathematical guarantee from the observed performance of an implementation.

The paper also fully characterizes the relaxed problem’s local minima in terms of the original balanced cut problem. This connects the continuous objective back to the discrete clustering task that motivated it. Relating that characterization to algorithm convergence helps explain both where optimization can settle and how those destinations correspond to the underlying partitioning problem.
neurips-2012-convergence-and-energy-land.tldr: The paper proves convergence results for two Cheeger Cut algorithms and characterizes how relaxed local minima relate to balanced cuts.

paragraphs: Subspace learning compresses data into a low-dimensional representation while preserving the ability to reconstruct it accurately. When observations come from multiple sources, such as different camera angles or text paired with images, the representation must account for relationships across those sources. The paper focuses on conditional independence constraints imposed on their shared latent representation.

The authors formulate multi-view subspace learning as a convex problem that enforces these constraints while reducing dimensionality. Respecting the structure of the separate views can improve the learned representation. Their algorithm exploits an implicit convex regularizer to obtain an optimal reconstruction, making the structural constraint part of the optimization rather than an informal modeling preference.

The procedure then jointly and optimally recovers the corresponding latent representation and reconstruction model. These optimality claims concern the proposed formulation. Experiments illustrate high-quality results, supporting the usefulness of combining reconstruction, dimensionality reduction, and conditional independence in a single framework. The contribution is both a structured way to combine views and an efficient algorithm for solving that formulation.
neurips-2012-convex-multi-view-subspace-.tldr: A convex formulation learns compact representations from multiple data sources while enforcing conditional independence and optimizing reconstruction.

paragraphs: The paper uses video to learn image features that remain stable as appearances change. It begins by detecting salient features and tracking them over time, simulating visual fixation and smooth pursuit. These tracked sequences provide the input to a hierarchical network, connecting the learning signal to observations that follow the same visual content.

The network learns through a temporal slowness constraint, which encourages its features to change slowly across the tracked sequence. Successive levels of the hierarchy encode increasingly complex invariances. Although video supplies the training signal, the resulting features are spatial, so they can be extracted from individual still images without requiring a video sequence at use time.

The authors evaluate the features on COIL-100, Caltech 101, STL-10, and PubFig, reporting consistent classification accuracy improvements of 4% to 5%. They also report 61% recognition accuracy on STL-10, described as state of the art. These findings support using tracked temporal experience to learn representations useful for static image recognition.
neurips-2012-deep-learning-of-invariant-.tldr: Tracking salient content in video trains hierarchical invariant features that improve classification when applied to still images.

paragraphs: Contour detection identifies boundaries in images and supports tasks such as segmentation and object recognition. Many approaches measure contrast with manually designed gradient features. This paper instead learns representations of image patches through sparse coding, then measures contrast between those representations. The resulting Sparse Code Gradients make the description of local appearance part of what is learned.

The method uses K-SVD to learn a dictionary and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit to encode patches. Multi-scale pooling and power transforms represent oriented local neighborhoods before gradients are computed and a linear support vector machine is applied. Keeping richer patch information until the contrast computation helps the method learn how to distinguish contour-relevant local differences.

On BSDS500, the reported F-measure rises from 0.71 for gPb contours to 0.74. The authors also apply the approach to depth images and surface normals, reporting promising depth-only and depth-plus-color results on the NYU Depth Dataset. These findings show that learned contrast representations can improve contour detection and adapt to additional sensor information.
neurips-2012-discriminatively-trained-sp.tldr: Sparse Code Gradients learn local contrast representations that improve contour detection and extend to depth-based imagery.

paragraphs: This paper studies online expert selection across k sites that communicate through a coordinator. On each round, one site chooses an expert and observes every expert’s payoff for that round. The system must keep regret low while limiting communication, so information sharing becomes a resource to manage alongside prediction quality.

Full communication achieves regret O(√(log(n)T)) using T communication, while independent learning without communication gives O(√(log(n)kT)) regret. The authors investigate the difficulty of improving simultaneously on the √(kT) regret scale and the T communication scale. For an oblivious adversary, their algorithm achieves regret O(√(k^(5(1+ε)/6)T)) with communication O(T/k^ε), for 0 < ε < 1/5.

This result provides a tunable intermediate trade-off: reducing communication changes the regret guarantee. The paper also studies a different arrangement in which the coordinator chooses the expert. In that version, an existing label-efficient forecaster already gives a nearly optimal regret–communication trade-off. Thus, who makes the decision materially affects the distributed learning problem.
neurips-2012-distributed-non-stochastic-.tldr: The paper characterizes communication–regret tensions in distributed expert selection and gives an intermediate trade-off against an oblivious adversary.

paragraphs: Objects in the same category can have substantially different shapes, while background clutter makes their parts difficult to identify. This paper represents object shape using a discriminative And-Or graph. The model combines local evidence with choices among alternative parts and a final check of the overall object.

Its three layers have distinct roles. Leaf nodes localize parts and are connected by collaborative edges. Or-nodes select among leaf nodes, while the root performs global verification. A learning algorithm extended from CCCP adjusts both the multilayer parameters and the graph structure during training, including which leaf nodes belong to particular or-nodes.

Learning the structure dynamically reduces the need for elaborate supervision and initialization. The authors report that the model handles large within-class variation and clutter, and that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on challenging datasets including INRIA-Horse, ETHZ-Shape, and UIUC-People. The stated results support treating the arrangement of alternative parts as something to learn together with the parameters used to recognize them.
neurips-2012-dynamical-and-or-graph-lear.tldr: A dynamically learned And-Or graph combines alternative object parts and global verification to detect shapes amid variation and clutter.

paragraphs: Spiking-network models of Bayesian inference and unsupervised learning often depend on specially formatted inputs or complicated neuronal and synaptic computations. This paper investigates whether homeostatic processes can ease those requirements. Its mathematical treatment gives such processes a direct role in implementing probabilistic learning, beyond merely accompanying synaptic change.

The central result interprets homeostatic plasticity as enforcing a balancing constraint on the posterior during inference and Expectation Maximization learning. Connecting these dynamics to variational inference shows that difficult terms appearing in a broad class of probabilistic models disappear under the framework. This explains how balancing activity can simplify the computations required by existing models.

The authors demonstrate feasibility in a spiking Winner-Take-All architecture for Bayesian inference and learning. They also outline how the framework could extend to richer recurrent networks; that extension is presented as a sketch. Overall, the theory links homeostatic dynamics and synaptic plasticity through a shared probabilistic interpretation and points toward an essential role for homeostasis in these spiking-network computations.
neurips-2012-homeostatic-plasticity-in-b.tldr: Homeostatic plasticity can enforce posterior balancing constraints that simplify Bayesian inference and learning in spiking networks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic model for understanding legislative voting through the issues discussed in bills. The model uses bill text to uncover lawmakers’ positions on particular political topics. Linking the content of legislation to voting behavior makes it possible to examine political positions in a space with several dimensions.

A central use is exploring departures from expected voting patterns. The model asks how a lawmaker’s deviation depends on what a bill concerns, giving those departures an issue-specific interpretation. To estimate the model, the authors derive approximate posterior inference algorithms using variational methods, connecting the observed legislative data to the underlying positions the model seeks to describe.

Evaluation across twelve years of legislative data demonstrates improved prediction on heldout observations and usefulness for interpreting the multidimensional political space. These are complementary outcomes: the model supports predictions of unseen voting data while also organizing behavior by issue. The findings support using legislative text as substantive information for understanding how lawmakers’ voting patterns vary across topics.
neurips-2012-how-they-vote-issue-adjuste.tldr: A probabilistic model uses bill text to explain issue-dependent voting patterns and improve heldout prediction.

paragraphs: When people search memory, related items tend to appear together in clusters. One explanation compares this behavior to animals searching for food in patches: people explore a group of related memories, then decide to leave as that group becomes depleted. This account assigns separate roles to searching within a cluster and switching between clusters.

The paper shows that the findings used to support that explanation also arise from a random walk on a semantic network. In this alternative, retrieval follows links between related items through a single process. The network’s organization allows clustered retrieval and movement between clusters to emerge without adding a separate rational switching decision.

The result offers a simpler, unified account of the observed memory-search patterns. It shows that those patterns can be explained by more than one underlying mechanism. The authors also connect the model conceptually to the random web surfer used in internet search, suggesting that studying memory representations and retrieval processes could potentially inform other information-retrieval settings.
neurips-2012-human-memory-search-as-a-ra.tldr: A random walk through a semantic network reproduces memory-search patterns previously attributed to separate exploration and switching processes.

paragraphs: Hyperalignment addresses the problem of aligning several datasets through a multi-set orthogonal Procrustes formulation. This paper introduces Kernel Hyperalignment, a regularized extension that uses kernels. Its purpose is to broaden both the kinds of similarity alignment can express and the size of the feature sets it can handle.

The kernel extension allows nonlinear similarity measures to enter the alignment problem. It also enables alignment when each dataset contains many base features. These capabilities matter together: an alignment method can be useful for rich datasets only if its representation of similarity and its handling of feature dimensionality suit the data being compared.

The paper applies this framework to functional MRI data from multiple subjects. It identifies large regions of interest, including the entire cortex, as suitable targets for the method. Experiments use real-world multi-subject fMRI data. The stated contribution is therefore an expanded alignment framework with a concrete neuroimaging application, connecting nonlinear similarity modeling to the demands of aligning large brain datasets.
neurips-2012-kernel-hyperalignment-f2004.tldr: Kernel Hyperalignment extends multi-dataset alignment to nonlinear similarities and large feature sets, with applications to multi-subject fMRI.

paragraphs: Predicting molecular energies accurately is important for rational compound design. Molecular data presents a particular learning challenge because its structure is naturally graph-like, rather than a straightforward vector of measurements. This paper takes a learning-from-scratch approach, predicting quantum-mechanical molecular energies directly from raw molecular geometry.

The study examines how representation choices support that prediction task. Its findings suggest benefits from flexible priors and from enforcing invariance stochastically rather than building it structurally into the model. Invariance concerns keeping the representation or prediction insensitive to changes that should not alter the relevant molecular information. The paper presents the benefit of this design choice as a suggestion supported by the study.

The authors report an improvement over the state of the art by a factor of almost three. They describe this as progress toward chemical accuracy, rather than a claim that the target has been reached. The broader significance is evidence that learning representations directly from geometry can substantially improve statistical prediction of molecular energetics.
neurips-2012-learning-invariant-represen.tldr: Learning directly from molecular geometry substantially improves energy prediction, with results suggesting benefits from flexible priors and stochastic invariance.

paragraphs: The paper studies data generated by a mixture of discrete graphical models. The component responsible for each observation is hidden, and different components may have different dependency graphs as well as different parameters. Learning therefore requires disentangling several underlying models without being told which observations belong to which component.

The authors propose a method with provable guarantees for estimating the mixture components. Its output is a mixture of tree models that provides a good approximation to the underlying graphical-model mixture. This distinction matters because the original components need not all be trees: the learned tree mixture is also an approximation tool for a broader class of structures.

For a mixture with r components and p variables, both sample requirements and computation scale polynomially in p and r over the stated model class. That class includes tree mixtures and mixtures of bounded-degree graphs. The result connects theoretical learnability with computational feasibility, showing that hidden component assignments and differing structures can be handled together for this range of models.
neurips-2012-learning-mixtures-of-tree-g.tldr: A provably supported method learns tree-mixture approximations of discrete graphical-model mixtures with polynomial sample and computational requirements.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection often measures how unusual a sample is using one notion of dissimilarity, such as Euclidean distance. Some datasets contain unusual patterns that no single measure captures adequately. Combining several criteria with a weighted sum offers one approach, but unknown criterion importance can force repeated runs with different weight choices.

The paper introduces Pareto depth analysis, a nonparametric method for detecting anomalies across multiple criteria. It uses Pareto optimality to retain the comparison across criteria without repeatedly choosing weighted combinations. This changes how conflicting dissimilarity signals are handled: the method works with their joint ordering instead of requiring one fixed scalar summary.

The authors report that the approach scales linearly with the number of criteria and establish a provable advantage over linear combinations of those criteria. These contributions address both the cost of adding criteria and the drawbacks of exploring weight settings. The method is especially motivated by settings where several dissimilarity measures are meaningful but their relative importance is not known beforehand.
neurips-2012-multi-criteria-anomaly-dete.tldr: Pareto depth analysis detects anomalies using multiple criteria without repeated weight selection and has a proved advantage over linear combinations.

paragraphs: This paper considers estimating the means of several independent datasets together. The proposed method, multi-task averaging, combines the separate sample averages through a multi-task learning approach. Each resulting estimate is a convex combination of the single-task averages, so the method shares information by taking weighted averages of those individual estimates.

A central question is how much regularization to apply when forming the joint estimates. The authors derive an optimal amount and show that it can be estimated effectively. This makes the strength of information sharing part of the method itself, rather than leaving the entire decision to an external search over tuning values.

Simulations and real-data experiments evaluate MTA alongside maximum likelihood and James-Stein estimators. The abstract’s sentence describing that comparison is incomplete, so it does not clearly state the comparative outcome. It does explicitly report that estimating regularization rivals cross-validation in performance while requiring less computation. That finding supports the practical value of deriving a direct regularization estimate for joint mean estimation.
neurips-2012-multi-task-averaging-6f5e90.tldr: Multi-task averaging jointly estimates dataset means, with an efficient regularization estimate reported to rival cross-validation.

paragraphs: The paper compares five ways to classify observations into multiple categories: One vs. All, All Pairs, tree-based classifiers, randomly coded Error Correcting Output Codes, and Multiclass SVM. The first four build multiclass decisions from binary classifiers. The analysis considers binary hypothesis classes with VC dimension d, including halfspaces in d-dimensional real space.

The comparison separates estimation error from approximation error. Estimation error concerns learning from a limited sample, while approximation error concerns what a chosen hypothesis class can represent. Studying both allows the authors to examine how the construction of a multiclass classifier affects its possibilities as well as its demands on data.

A distinctive feature is using tools from VC theory to analyze approximation error, whereas earlier applications largely focused on estimation error. The analysis yields conclusions about the success of different methods under different conditions. Its practical value lies in identifying condition-dependent differences among common approaches, rather than presenting a single multiclass construction as universally preferable.
neurips-2012-multiclass-learning-approac.tldr: A theoretical comparison of five multiclass methods examines both estimation and approximation error, using VC theory in an unusual role.

paragraphs: Sparsity-inducing penalties encourage a model to use a limited set of nonzero quantities. This paper studies nonconvex penalties through a probabilistic construction based on Lévy processes. It defines a penalty as the Laplace exponent of a subordinator, providing a systematic route for constructing such penalties from stochastic-process objects.

The authors establish two concrete correspondences. The logarithmic penalty is the Laplace exponent of a Gamma subordinator, while the exponential penalty is the Laplace exponent of a compound Poisson subordinator. These results place two named penalties within the same construction framework, connecting their mathematical forms to different underlying processes.

The paper also examines the penalties through concave conjugates, an alternative mathematical representation. Both logarithmic and exponential penalties arise as concave conjugates of negative Kullback-Leibler distance functions. Their relationship is traced to the asymmetry of that distance. Together, these connections explain the penalties from both stochastic-process and conjugate perspectives, with the contribution centered on construction and mathematical relationships rather than an empirical performance comparison.
neurips-2012-nonconvex-penalization-usin.tldr: The paper constructs nonconvex sparsity penalties from stochastic processes and links logarithmic and exponential penalties through concave conjugates and KL asymmetry.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks reward functions that explain observed behavior. Many earlier approaches assume that all behavior comes from an agent optimizing one reward function. This paper addresses the practical difficulty of that assumption by allowing the observations to reflect multiple underlying reward functions.

The authors integrate a Dirichlet process mixture model into Bayesian inverse reinforcement learning. The mixture formulation gives the model a way to represent several reward functions within one probabilistic account of the behavior data. Its nonparametric Bayesian structure is central to extending the single-reward formulation to this multiple-reward setting.

To estimate the rewards, the paper develops an efficient Metropolis-Hastings sampling algorithm that uses the gradient of the posterior. Experiments across several problem domains show better performance than previous approaches. The stated findings support explicitly modeling multiple rewards when a single shared objective is difficult to justify. The contribution joins that modeling change with an inference procedure designed to make estimation practical, rather than stopping at a more expressive probabilistic description.
neurips-2012-nonparametric-bayesian-inve.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture extends Bayesian inverse reinforcement learning to multiple reward functions and improves results across several tested domains.

paragraphs: The paper studies multilabel prediction and ranking when the learner receives only partial information. An algorithm in this setting must make useful predictions while also acquiring information that can improve later decisions. The proposed method combines second-order descent with upper-confidence bounds to manage this exploration–exploitation trade-off.

The analysis allows the covariates, or input features, to be adversarial. It assumes, however, that multilabel probabilities follow linear or generalized linear models. Under this partially adversarial setup, the authors establish regret bounds of O(√T log T), reporting improvements over existing results in several respects. The modeling assumption is part of the setting in which the guarantee applies.

Experiments on real-world multilabel datasets compare the confidence-based scheme with baselines that receive full information. The partial-feedback method often reaches comparable performance, providing empirical support for its information-selection strategy. Together, the theory and experiments show how confidence-guided exploration can support effective multilabel learning despite incomplete feedback, without claiming equivalence to full-information learning in every case.
neurips-2012-on-multilabel-classificatio.tldr: A confidence-guided second-order algorithm learns multilabel predictions from partial feedback, with regret guarantees under a partially adversarial model.

paragraphs: Object detectors often search an image by evaluating many sliding windows. This straightforward approach can spend substantial effort on uninformative locations. The paper develops sequential search strategies that choose the next window based on what earlier windows revealed, making the search responsive to both the object category and the particular image.

The guiding information is context learned from training data. Specifically, the method uses statistical relationships between a window’s appearance and its position relative to an object. An observation can therefore help direct attention toward other locations, even as the search proceeds. Window selection becomes an adaptive process informed by accumulated visual evidence.

On PASCAL VOC 2010, the authors report evaluating two orders of magnitude fewer windows while also achieving higher detection accuracy. This combines a reduction in search effort with improved detection in the reported experiment. The finding supports the idea that learning where to look can be as consequential as evaluating what appears at a predetermined set of locations.
neurips-2012-searching-for-objects-drive.tldr: Context-guided sequential search evaluates roughly 100 times fewer windows while improving detection accuracy on PASCAL VOC 2010.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes asking whether two datasets come from exactly the same distribution from asking whether their distributions are similar. With finite samples, similarity is a useful target in its own right. The authors introduce a discrepancy score, perturbed variation, intended to express that relationship directly.

The score interprets similarity through an optimal perturbation that makes the distributions fit each other as well as possible. Although defined for distributions, it can be estimated efficiently from observed samples. The authors provide convergence bounds for the estimate, linking the sample-based calculation to the distribution-level quantity it aims to measure.

They also develop hypothesis tests for whether two datasets come from similar distributions. Simulations examine the tests’ statistical power, and real-data comparisons assess how the score detects similarity relative to other measures. These evaluations accompany a contribution that spans a definition of similarity, an efficient estimator, and statistical testing procedures, making the proposed notion usable with finite observations.
neurips-2012-the-perturbed-variation-b47.tldr: Perturbed variation measures distributional similarity through optimal perturbations and supports efficient estimation and hypothesis testing from samples.
